# More on Strings

This page will go into more detail about string data, with some useful tips and tricks for handling it in your programs...

## Arithmetic operators and strings

Here are the most important operators that we looked at on the [Expressions](1_06_Expressions) page.

| Expression Type | Operator | Example    | Value     |
|-----------------|----------|------------|-----------|
| Addition        | `+`      | `2 + 3`    | `5`       |
| Subtraction     | `-`      | `2 - 3`    | `-1`      |
| Multiplication  | `*`      | `2 * 3`    | `6`       |
| Division        | `/`      | `100 / 10` | `10`      |
| Remainder       | `%`      | `101 % 10` | `1`       |
| Exponentiation (Power)  | `**`     | `10 ** 2`  | `100`  

In the cellow, try these out with different strings. See what happens, see which ones you can use with string and which ones you cannot. There is an example in the cell already.

```{python}
# Your code here
"We already know that we can" + " add strings together!"
```

Experiment with strings yourself in the code cell above, before you read the page below...

....



.....



......



.......

If you did experiment with strings, you will have found that `+` and `*` operators work with string literals, in expressions. All the other arithmetic operators (`*`, `/`, `%`) cause an error.

```{python}
# This works.
"It is just one string" + " after another."
```

```{python}
# This also works. Note: this only works if the second literal is a number, not another string.
"It is one string after another! " * 10
```

```{python tags=c("raises-exception")}
# This does NOT work.
"It is just one string" / " after another."
```

```{python tags=c("raises-exception")}
# This does NOT work.
"It is just one string" ** " after another."
```

## Multi-line strings

We can use 3 quotation marks (`'` or `"`) instead of one, so that we can make long strings, without needing loads of `print()` functions!:

```{python}
print("This is a string on one line.")
```

```{python}
# Look at the three quotation marks (""") at the start and end of the string.
print("""       
This string...

...can go over...

...as many lines...

...as I want...
""")
```

## F-strings

We have already seen how to put numbers and text together using lots of `+` symbols and the `str` function.

A better way to do this is to use *f-strings*. F-strings are *very* useful. They take some time to get used to, but you will find them very helpful for showing results and debugging your code.

To use a f-string, just put at "f" at the start of your string!:

```{python}
f"This is an f-string!"
```

Now, inside our f-string, if we put variables, literals or expressions inside curly brackets `{}`, they will become part of the string:

```{python}
# Make variable.
number_of_students = 17
```

```{python}
# Look -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------> HERE!
f"This is an f-string! It can show the value of my `number_of_students` variable like this: {number_of_students}"
```

```{python}
f"We can also put literals/expressions inside our string, like this: {8 * 100}" 
```

Note that using "f" before the string is allowed in Python, because the Python compiler knows it means "this is an f-string! Let me put variables in it!". However, we will get errors if we use other letters, as the Python compiler does not know what these mean:

```{python tags=c("raises-exception")}
e"This is not allowed!"
```

If you want to, you can launch this page on Binder or Live code, and use the cell below to play around with f-strings:

```{python}
# You can use this cell to play with f-strings.
my_variable = 10

print(f"Here is an example f-string. I can use square brackets to show a variable, like this variable: {my_variable}")
```
